subject: physics

unit.name: System of Particles and Rotational Motion

chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
question_text: State and prove the perpendicular axes theorem.

verification.note: Sri Chaitanya IPE Junior Fastrack (Rev. May 2024), Unit 7 SHORT ANSWER. The mark split is invented and needs a Telangana IPE teacher; no exam appearance years are printed, so appearances[] stays empty.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The statement
lines: For a PLANE lamina, the sum of the
moments of inertia about two mutually
perpendicular axes in its plane equals
the moment of inertia about the axis
steps.margin_note: Say "plane lamina" — the theorem is for flat bodies only, and the examiner checks for the word.
steps.why: This theorem is flat-body-only because it needs every particle to have z = 0; for a solid body the proof line r² = x² + y² fails.
common_mistakes: Applying it to a sphere or cylinder — it holds only for a plane lamina.

recall.must_convey: That for a plane lamina, I_z = I_x + I_y for two perpendicular in-plane axes and the normal axis through their intersection.
accept: I z equals I x plus I y
two perpendicular axes in the plane
reject: I equals I naught plus M r squared

steps.memory_tip: I_z = I_x + I_y — and say "plane lamina": the theorem works only for flat bodies.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: x and y in the plane of the lamina, z coming out of it, one particle at P with its x and y distances shown.
steps.why: The one line the proof needs — r² = x² + y² — is visible in the figure as the right triangle O, foot, P.
common_mistakes: Drawing z inside the plane. z must be perpendicular to the lamina.

recall.must_convey: That a figure is drawn with x, y in the lamina plane, z perpendicular, and a particle P at distance r.
accept: draw the lamina with x y z axes
figure with particle P and r
reject: I z equals I x plus I y

steps.memory_tip: Draw the lamina in the xy-plane with one particle at (x, y); the right triangle shows r² = x² + y².

steps.label: The proof
lines: Take a particle of mass m at P, at
distance r from O, with coordinates
(x, y). Since the lamina lies in the
Moment of inertia about the z-axis:
steps.margin_note: One particle first, then the sum over all particles — the same two-beat shape as the parallel axes proof.
steps.why: Distance from the z-axis is r; distance from the x-axis is y; distance from the y-axis is x. The Pythagoras line converts one sum into the other two.
common_mistakes: Writing I_x = Σmx² — the distance from the x-axis is y, so I_x = Σmy².

recall.must_convey: That r² = x² + y² for each particle, so summing gives I_z as two sums.
accept: r squared is x squared plus y squared
sigma m r squared splits into two sums

steps.label: The result
lines: But Σmy² = I_x and Σmx² = I_y, so
steps.margin_note: Name each sum as it becomes I_x or I_y — that line carries the mark, not the final box alone.
steps.why: The proof is two definitions and one Pythagoras — which is why the theorem costs so little and appears so often.
common_mistakes: Swapping which sum is I_x and which is I_y.

recall.must_convey: That naming the two sums as I_x and I_y gives I_z = I_x + I_y.
accept: sigma m y squared is I x
so I z equals I x plus I y
reject: r squared is x squared plus y squared

steps.memory_tip: Name the sums back carefully: Σmy² = I_x and Σmx² = I_y — the distance FROM the x-axis is y.
